title: We Do Not Swear Unconditional Obedience - emptywheel

by Peterr | Sep 11, 2026 | 2026 Mid-Term Election, 2028 Presidential election, Department of Justice, Featured, Making Good Trouble, Trump 2.0, Trump Administration | 52 comments

Leni Riefenstahl, the filmmaker of the Third Reich

I only saw brief clips of the Trumpapalooza, but one of the few I saw brought me up short. From Aaron Rupar on Bluesky (with video at the link), describing a point where Trump asked the crowd to stand:

Trump: “Please right your right hand. I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States. That loves us so much he can’t even breath. That I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way – I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell…”

I physically shuddered as Trump began that pledge, because it reminded me so much of another pledge to another ruler. The photo below shows the pledge, as it appears in the Evangelisches Feldgesangbuch, the protestant field hymnal for the German Wehrmacht. The same pledge appears in the Katolisches Feldgesangbuch, which was the Roman Catholic military hymnal.

The German Soldier’s Oath, August 1939

The text translates like this:

I swear by God this holy oath, that I will render unconditional obedience to the Führer of the German Reich and people, Adolf Hitler, Supreme Commander of the Wehrmacht, and that, as a brave soldier, I will be prepared to risk my life at any time for this oath.

They were published in August 1939 by the Luftwaffe, and handed out to the soldiers of the German military. Right before they invaded Poland the following month.

It wasn’t always like this. During the Weimar Republic, members of the military swore an oath to the German constitution, but after the death in 1934 of President Paul von Hindenberg, the oath changed. It became a pledge to Adolf Hitler personally, the leader of the state and the leader of the people. Shortly thereafter, civilian members of the government were made to take a similar oath.

I lived in Germany for a time as an exchange student, right after they showed the NBC miniseries “The Holocaust” on national television. It was the first time there was such a public discussion of that subject, telling the story from Kristallnacht to the ghettos and finally to the death camps and gas chambers. I had conversations with old women whose husbands, fathers, uncles, brothers, and sons had gone off to war, with middle-aged folks who were kids at the time (including men who had been part of the Hilter youth as young boys – much the way that young American boys would join the Cub Scouts – “it’s what everyone did at that age”), and especially with my classmates at school. Beyond the horrors of the Holocaust itself, the stories of the cult of personality were gripping. “How could you have allowed that to happen?” said the folks my age to their grandparents, who mainly had little answer. A few talked about being connected with the “Confessing Church” which opposed the Deutsche Christen, the nationalistic Aryan folks who tried to take over German religious life. But for most, the older folks felt embarrassed at best, if not guilty and ashamed.

“I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States . . .”

So yeah, I shuddered when I heard those words. Shuddered, not in surprise but in pain. Trump has made it clear that he expects this kind of unconditional obedience from the attorneys of the DOJ, and Todd Blanche has done his best to clean out those who do not share that view of the DOJ’s attorneys. Pete Hegseth, the Secretary of Excursions, has the same mentality at the DOD, and has similarly worked hard to clean house of problematic generals and admirals. When Trump rails at the Supreme Court, it carries clear anger that the justices he nominated and got onto the court are not living up to an oath demanding unconditional obedience to him personally, even if they never actually took such an oath.

Or look at how Trump reacted to Senator Mark Kelly and his former military and intelligence community colleagues, when they pointed out that in our military, we not only do NOT demand unconditional obedience, but we demand exactly the opposite. Soldiers who are given illegal orders are not just given permission to disregard these orders but are REQUIRED not to obey them. Oh, the horror, says Trump, and he sicced DOJ and the DOD to go after Kelly et al., threatening not only their ranks and their pensions, but their very liberty.

That’s how Trump views being president. Everyone owes him — not the country or the constitution or the law, but him — unconditional obedience. And look at what he demanded his obedient minions do: cheat like hell.

Here in Missouri, we’ve seen what demands for unconditional obedience can do. We’ve been dealing with more than just the gerrymandering mess, but also anti-abortion zealots, some of the worst anti-trans laws in the country, and ballot measures that would have neutered the ability of the voters to use initiative petitions to overturn the most idiotic laws the legislature comes up with.

When a leader — any leader — demands unconditional obedience, be afraid. In a religious setting, that’s when you get to Jim Jones or pedophile priests. In an academic setting, this is when you get researchers who twist their data to fit the views of their superiors rather than letting it speak honestly. In a military setting, this is when you get My Lai. In a political setting, this is when you get Adolf Hitler.

We have less than 8 weeks before the elections in November. Many of the races are between candidates who act as if they have sworn unconditional obedience to Trump and candidates who have not. I envision my hypothetical grandkids asking me “How could you have allowed that to happen?”

I don’t want to shrug my shoulders in embarrassment, or bow my head in guilt and shame. And neither should you. It’s time to keep making good trouble.

Corporations have no obligation to obey EOs, yet they’re so afraid of him that they will.

The don’t have an immediate obligation in the way that federal employees have, but they still have secondary obligations.

Corporate lawyers will tell the CEO that they have a fiduciary obligation to their board and their shareholders to protect their investment. If you fight Trump, it will cost you a lot and you may get in trouble for tanking their investment. “Resist the EO and lose all federal contracts” is a helluva threat, especially for a company who depends on such contracts.

Of course, selling your soul comes with a cost too. Just ask some of those formerly big “Big Law” firms who bent the knee, only to see partners, associates, and clients head for the door. “I want a law firm who stands up for me, and you’ve proven unwilling to stand up even for yourselves, so I’ll look elsewhere for representation.”

Corporations and other institutions are learning — sometimes the hard way — that it is increasingly difficult for them to try to avoid taking a stand. It’s not “Will you take a stand?” but “Where will you stand?”

This maxim – [the only legitimate purpose of a corporation is to maximize shareholder value] – is now accepted as an article of faith in finance and the corporate legal profession. It wasn’t always so, and in fact the law has never been so. It was merely an assertion made by Milt Friedman around 1970, and when his Chicago School of economics seeped its way into the mainstream, that mythical assertion came with it.

IMO, the Chicago School has proven a failure, Friedman’s Nobel Prize notwithstanding. It, and this pernicious maxim, should be cast into the dustbin where it belongs.

Years ago this phenomenon was more frustrating, but always tempered with the expectation that the media would evolve to a better place in covering Trump. Now it’s just more of bleak despair.

Some corporate-owned media is covering it, but they are both sanitizing/sane-washing it and amplifying Trump’s message.

As I told the emptywheel team,

I can’t avoid exposure to broadcast TV here at my Mom’s. I don’t know which national network she had on but they gave a driveby report on Trump’s demand of his MAGAts at Trump-a-palooza; they conveniently omitted his request that his adherents commit election fraud and cheat.

It’s literally amplification and dispersion of his demand for criminal behavior, complicity in incitement. It’s seditious.

And FCC’s Carr doesn’t have a problem with this — just candidate Talarico on ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel.

The network I heard walked up to the point where Trump called for election fraud, so that his call to his base to do as he asked was pushed but the worst part of the crazy which is clearly a call for unlawful behavior was cut.

The other problem beyond deliberate sanewashing is media exhaustion.

From the standpoint of editors/producers, they’ve got a dog-bites-man problem in covering Trump. If every outrageous thing Trump said is given lead story OMG coverage, there’d be OMG outrage every day and twice on Sundays. At some point, the outrage becomes background noise. “Oh, Trump opened his mouth again. Yawn.”

I can sympathize with this to a point, but if they NEVER express outrage about anything, then they are becoming complicit in his communications.

I’ve been thinking long and hard about this post, Peterr.

You’ve mentioned your experience as an exchange student in Germany [was it Stuttgart?] several times over the years I’ve been a community member here,
and I think you were a high school student at the time. According to the Wiki you link to here, that must have been in 1979 [or maybe 1980]. Also, you’ve mentioned that your father grew up in a bi-lingual family and moved to a new home in 1943 where the children were admonished not to speak German in public. I don’t know when your ancestors immigrated.

I was a college-age exchange student in Germany in 1976-77. [My two previous visits had been at the ages of 2 and 9.] My parents immigrated from northwestern Germany [Nieder Sachsen] in 1955. We did not speak German at home. My parents learned English from scratch but spoke their Platt Deutsch dialect to each other.
My older brother and I absorbed some of that as we were learning to speak.
[I can still understand but not speak it.]

So, those “old women whose husbands, fathers, uncles, brothers, and sons had gone off to war” were my grandmothers and great Aunts. Those “middle-aged folks who were kids at the time” were my parents, aunts and uncles. And your “classmates at school” were my younger cousins.

“How could you have allowed that to happen?” said the folks my age to their grandparents, who mainly had little answer. […] the older folks felt embarrassed at best, if not guilty and ashamed.”

I’m sorry, but I can maybe understand a high school kid asking that question in that way and interpreting their grandparents’ response in that way.

But surely, you as a “hypothetical grandparent” realize that we, right now, do not “allow [this clusterfuck] to happen”, and that maybe most of them didn’t either.

The experiences I shared are just that: the impressions of the conversations in Germany of which I was a part, or that my friends and classmates told me about. Decades of communal national silence had just been broken, which arose and persisted after the end of the war because even talking about the pre-war era stirred up such ugly memories. For many, it was easier not to talk, because then you don’t have to discuss the “if only” nightmares of your past. But when that miniseries was broadcast, not talking was no longer an option.

Even if the folks had been active in opposing the Nazis, the “if I only did more” thoughts are as bad for those people as the “if I had only done something” thoughts of others. On another level, the embarrassment was cultural: “Germany used to be respected, but after what our leaders did, we are now a global embarrassment if not pariah.” This was also only seven years after the Munich Olympics, where the PLO terrorists embarrassed the West German military and police in their attack on Israeli athletes in the Olympic village.

As an exchange student, more than once I went into small local shops where Mr and Mrs Ugly American were being abusive toward a shopkeeper (“Why don’t they speak English?” or “Maybe if I speak more loudly they will understand me . . .”), and after they finished their business and left, the shopkeeper turned to me. Though I could pass as a German at the time, I also offered my apologies for the conduct of my fellow Americans who had proceeded me.

Going back to today, I think about Americans who travel to Canada or who (like me) engage with Canadian friends and colleagues. I can both be very actively opposing Trump and feel like I need to apologize for my nation to my friends.

Embarrassment by association with an authoritarian is not eliminated by being someone who stands up to an authoritarian.
